name: Religion in Stuart England
summary: How the Church of England, Puritans, Catholics, Scots Presbyterians, and new sects fought over worship and church government from James I's accession to Queen Anne's death, through civil war, the abolition and restoration of bishops, the Great Ejection, the Glorious Revolution, and the Toleration Act.

start.label: James VI of Scotland succeeds Elizabeth I as James I of England; Puritans soon present the Millenary Petition

end.label: Queen Anne dies, the last Stuart monarch; the Protestant succession passes to George I of Hanover

key_dates.label: Hampton Court Conference answers the Puritans' Millenary Petition and agrees on a new Bible translation
Gunpowder Plot by Catholic conspirators to blow up Parliament is discovered
Authorized (King James) Version of the Bible published
Scottish National Covenant signed after riots against Laud's Prayer Book
Charles I tried and beheaded; England becomes a republic
Jews informally readmitted under Cromwell; Parliament punishes the Quaker James Nayler for blasphemy
Act of Uniformity and Great Ejection of about 2,000 ministers
Titus Oates's invented 'Popish Plot' sets off anti-Catholic trials
Seven Bishops acquitted; William of Orange invades and James II flees
Toleration Act allows Trinitarian Protestant Dissenters to worship
Act of Settlement bars Catholics from the throne

background.text: Elizabeth I left a Protestant Church of England governed by bishops and the Book of Common Prayer; Puritans wanted further reform of ceremonies and some wanted to replace bishops with presbyteries, while Catholics (recusants) were fined and their priests treated as traitors.
James I had been raised in the Presbyterian Church of Scotland but favored bishops, summing up his view at Hampton Court as 'No bishop, no king'.

happened.text: In 1603 Puritan clergy presented the Millenary Petition, said to speak for a thousand ministers, asking for changes such as dropping the sign of the cross in baptism and the surplice. At the Hampton Court Conference (January 1604) James granted few of them, but accepted John Rainolds's proposal for a new translation of the Bible, published in 1611.
The 1604 canons required clergy to subscribe to the Prayer Book and the Thirty-Nine Articles; some dozens of ministers (estimates run to about 80) were deprived for refusing.

After the Gunpowder Plot (5 November 1605), in which Robert Catesby, Guy Fawkes, and other Catholics planned to blow up the king and Parliament, Parliament passed harsher recusancy laws and an Oath of Allegiance (1606) denying the pope's power to depose kings, which Pope Paul V forbade Catholics to take.
In 1612 Bartholomew Legate and Edward Wightman were burned for heresy (anti-Trinitarian and other beliefs), the last people burned for heresy in England.

Under Charles I, William Laud (archbishop of Canterbury from 1633) and his allies, called 'Arminians' by opponents, promoted ceremony, railed altars at the east end of churches, and the 'beauty of holiness', and used the Court of High Commission and Star Chamber against Puritan critics. Puritans saw this as a drift toward Rome.

Imposing a new Prayer Book on Scotland led to a riot in St Giles' Cathedral, Edinburgh (23 July 1637; the story of Jenny Geddes throwing a stool is tradition) and to the National Covenant (February 1638). The Glasgow Assembly (late 1638) abolished bishops in Scotland, and the Bishops' Wars (1639–40) that followed forced Charles to recall Parliament.

The Long Parliament (from 1640) impeached Laud, removed bishops from the House of Lords (1642), and after civil war began (1642) called the Westminster Assembly (1643), which wrote the Westminster Confession and Catechisms. Parliament made the Solemn League and Covenant with the Scots (1643), replaced the Prayer Book with the Directory for Public Worship (1645), and abolished bishops (1646).

Laud was executed in January 1645 and Charles I on 30 January 1649. Under the Commonwealth and Protectorate, Oliver Cromwell allowed wide liberty to Protestant groups (Independents, Baptists, and others), though not to Catholics, Anglican Prayer Book worship, or those judged blasphemous; Quakers, Ranters, Fifth Monarchists, and other sects multiplied.

After the Whitehall Conference (December 1655), called in answer to Menasseh ben Israel's petition, reached no formal decision, Cromwell let the small Jewish community in London worship and acquire a burial ground in 1656, an informal readmission 366 years after the expulsion of 1290.

After the Restoration of Charles II (1660), bishops and the Prayer Book returned. The Act of Uniformity (1662) ejected about 2,000 ministers, and the 'Clarendon Code' (Corporation Act 1661, Conventicle Act 1664, Five Mile Act 1665) restricted Dissenters. Charles's Declaration of Indulgence (1672) was withdrawn under pressure from Parliament, which passed the Test Act (1673) excluding Catholics and Dissenters from office.

Titus Oates's false story of a Jesuit 'Popish Plot' to murder Charles II (1678) led to the trials and executions of Catholics, including Archbishop Oliver Plunkett of Armagh (1681), and to the Exclusion Crisis over whether Charles's Catholic brother James could inherit the throne.

James II (1685–88), a Catholic, issued Declarations of Indulgence (1687 and 1688) suspending the penal laws for Catholics and Dissenters. When Archbishop William Sancroft and six bishops petitioned against reading the 1688 Declaration in churches, they were sent to the Tower and tried for seditious libel, and were acquitted on 30 June 1688.

William of Orange landed in November 1688 and James fled. The Bill of Rights (1689) barred Catholics from the throne, the Toleration Act (1689) let Trinitarian Protestant Dissenters worship in licensed meeting houses, and in Scotland bishops were abolished and the Presbyterian Church of Scotland established (1690).

Archbishop Sancroft, several bishops, and about 400 clergy who would not swear allegiance to William and Mary while James lived (the non-jurors) were deprived of their posts and formed a small separate church.

The Act of Settlement (1701) gave the succession to the Protestant heirs of Sophia of Hanover and required the monarch to be in communion with the Church of England. Under Anne, High Church and Low Church parties clashed, notably over the trial of Henry Sacheverell (1710), the Occasional Conformity Act (1711), and the Schism Act (1714).

participants.name: Richard Baxter

participants.role: Catholic archbishop of Armagh executed in 1681

outcomes.text: The King James Bible became the standard English Bible for some three centuries.

The Church of England survived with bishops and the Prayer Book, but English Protestantism was permanently divided between the established church and Dissenting Presbyterians, Congregationalists, Baptists, and Quakers, who had legal worship after 1689 but stayed barred from universities and most public office until the 19th century.
Catholics remained under penal laws, and the Catholic exclusion from the throne set in 1689 and 1701 remains in law, although a 2013 act lifted the bar on heirs marrying Catholics.
Scotland kept a Presbyterian established church, guaranteed in the Act of Union of 1707; Scottish Episcopalians became a separate, largely non-juring church.
The Westminster Confession, written for an English church that never adopted it, became the standard of Presbyterians worldwide.

condemnations_note: Church and state condemnations ran in every direction: popes condemned English oaths, Scottish Presbyterians deposed bishops, Parliament condemned an archbishop and a king, and the Restoration church ejected Puritans. A selection of the main ones is listed.

condemnations.reason: Catholics forbidden to take James I's Oath of Allegiance, as contrary to faith
condemnations.status: Never formally lifted; the oath was later replaced

condemnations.by: John King, Bishop of London, and Richard Neile, Bishop of Coventry and Lichfield
condemnations.reason: Bartholomew Legate and Edward Wightman condemned as heretics for anti-Trinitarian beliefs and handed to the state for burning
condemnations.status: Never reversed; they were the last burned for heresy in England

condemnations.by: General Assembly of the Church of Scotland at Glasgow
condemnations.reason: Scottish bishops deposed, some excommunicated, and episcopacy abolished
condemnations.status: Bishops restored in Scotland in 1661 and abolished again in 1689–90

condemnations.reason: Archbishops and bishops abolished in England and Wales

condemnations.by: Charles II and the Cavalier Parliament
condemnations.reason: About 2,000 ministers ejected for not accepting the Prayer Book and episcopal ordination
condemnations.status: Never reversed; Dissenters gained toleration in 1689

condemnations.authority: Act requiring oaths to William and Mary (1689)
condemnations.reason: Archbishop Sancroft, several bishops, and about 400 clergy deprived as non-jurors
condemnations.status: Never reversed; the non-juring church died out in the 19th century

persecution_note: Every party that held power used it against others: Catholics, Puritans, Laudians, Quakers, Covenanters, and Dissenters were all fined, imprisoned, or executed at some point between 1603 and 1689, and war in Ireland brought killings of Protestants and Catholics. Numbers for the Irish killings are disputed. After 1689 Protestant Dissenters had legal worship but Catholics and anti-Trinitarians did not.

persecution.title: Executions and fines of Catholics under James I and Charles I
persecution.summary: After the Gunpowder Plot the surviving plotters were hanged, drawn, and quartered (January 1606), as was the Jesuit superior Henry Garnet (May 1606), who had learned of the plot in confession. Catholic priests continued to be executed as traitors in smaller numbers than under Elizabeth, and recusants paid heavy fines.

responsible.name: James I and later Charles I
Robert Cecil, Earl of Salisbury
responsible.role: Secretary of State who led the investigation of the plot

responsible.name: Parliament
responsible.role: Passed the 1606 recusancy laws and Oath of Allegiance

persecution.outcome: Anti-Catholic feeling and 5 November commemorations became fixtures of English life.

persecution.title: Burning of Bartholomew Legate and Edward Wightman
persecution.summary: Legate, who denied the Trinity, was burned at Smithfield after James I questioned him personally; Wightman was burned at Lichfield after recanting at the stake at a first attempt and then withdrawing his recantation.

responsible.name: James I
responsible.role: King; questioned Legate and signed the writs for burning

responsible.name: Richard Neile
responsible.role: Bishop of Coventry and Lichfield; condemned Wightman

persecution.outcome: The last burnings for heresy in England.

persecution.title: Punishment of Puritan critics under Laud
persecution.summary: Star Chamber had the ears of the pamphleteers William Prynne, Henry Burton, and John Bastwick cut off in 1637 for attacking the bishops; Puritan ministers were suspended by the Court of High Commission, and many Puritans emigrated to New England.

responsible.name: William Laud
responsible.role: Archbishop of Canterbury and member of the courts

responsible.name: Court of Star Chamber
responsible.role: Royal court that passed the sentences

persecution.outcome: The Long Parliament released Prynne, Burton, and Bastwick (1640) and abolished both courts (1641).

persecution.title: Killings in Ireland: the 1641 rising and Drogheda
persecution.summary: In the Catholic rising of October 1641 Protestant settlers in Ulster were driven out and many killed, as at Portadown; modern estimates are about 4,000 killed directly, far below contemporary claims of over 100,000. In September 1649 Cromwell's army stormed Drogheda and killed most of the garrison, along with Catholic priests and some civilians, about 3,500 people in all by most counts.

responsible.name: Oliver Cromwell
responsible.role: Commander of the English army in Ireland, who ordered no quarter at Drogheda

persecution.outcome: Numbers and the extent of civilian deaths in both episodes remain disputed by historians.

persecution.title: Executions of William Laud and Charles I
persecution.summary: Laud was impeached by the Long Parliament in December 1640, imprisoned in the Tower, tried in 1644, and beheaded under an ordinance of attainder after the Lords would not convict him of treason. Charles I was tried by a High Court of Justice set up by the purged Commons and beheaded on 30 January 1649.

responsible.name: The Long Parliament
responsible.role: Impeached Laud and passed the attainder

responsible.name: William Prynne
responsible.role: Laud's former victim, who prepared the prosecution

responsible.name: High Court of Justice under John Bradshaw
Oliver Cromwell and the army leaders
responsible.role: Drove the king's trial and signed the death warrant

persecution.outcome: At the Restoration surviving regicides were executed; the 1662 Prayer Book added a service for King Charles the Martyr (removed in 1859).

persecution.title: Punishment of James Nayler
persecution.summary: After the Quaker James Nayler rode into Bristol with followers singing 'Holy, holy, holy', Parliament itself tried him and found him guilty of 'horrid blasphemy'. He was whipped through London, pilloried, had his tongue bored with a hot iron and his forehead branded with 'B', and was imprisoned.

responsible.name: Oliver Cromwell
responsible.role: Lord Protector; asked Parliament on what authority it acted but did not stop the punishment

persecution.outcome: Released in 1659; died in 1660. Thousands of Quakers were jailed in the 1650s and 1660s.

persecution.title: Prosecution of Dissenters under the Clarendon Code
persecution.summary: Ejected ministers and lay Dissenters were fined and imprisoned for holding services; Quakers suffered most, and hundreds died in prison. John Bunyan was jailed for about 12 years in Bedford.

responsible.name: Charles II and the Cavalier Parliament
Justices of the peace and informers
responsible.role: Enforced the laws for a share of the fines

persecution.outcome: Ended for Trinitarian Protestants by the Toleration Act of 1689.

persecution.title: Persecution of Covenanters in Scotland
persecution.summary: After bishops were restored in Scotland, Presbyterian ministers who would not conform held field meetings (conventicles), which were broken up by troops; risings in 1666 and 1679 were crushed, and in the 'Killing Time' of the 1680s Covenanters were shot without trial or executed. Covenanters murdered Archbishop James Sharp of St Andrews in 1679.

responsible.name: John Graham of Claverhouse
responsible.role: Officer who led troops against Covenanters

responsible.name: Covenanter group led by David Hackston and John Balfour

persecution.outcome: Ended with the Revolution of 1688–90; the number killed is disputed, and Presbyterians then ousted many Episcopal clergy.

persecution.title: Popish Plot trials
persecution.summary: On the false evidence of Titus Oates and other informers, about 22 Catholics, mostly priests and laymen accused of plotting to kill the king, were executed, among them Edward Coleman (1678), Viscount Stafford (1680), and Archbishop Oliver Plunkett (1681).

responsible.name: Chief Justice William Scroggs and the courts
Earl of Shaftesbury and the Whig opposition
responsible.role: Exploited the plot to push for excluding James from the throne

responsible.name: Charles II
responsible.role: King, who doubted the plot but let the executions go ahead

persecution.outcome: Oates was convicted of perjury in 1685, flogged, and imprisoned, but freed and pensioned after 1688.

victims_intro: A selection of named people executed for religious reasons, or in cases where religion was central, between 1603 and 1714. It is not complete: dozens of Catholic priests and many Covenanters are not listed.

victims.name: Henry Garnet
victims.executed: Hanged, drawn, and quartered at St Paul's Churchyard, London, 3 May 1606
victims.condemned_by: Court of King's Bench under James I
victims.allegation: Jesuit superior convicted of treason for not revealing the Gunpowder Plot, which he said he learned of under the seal of confession.

victims.name: Bartholomew Legate
victims.condemned_by: John King, Bishop of London; writ under James I

victims.name: Edward Wightman
victims.condemned_by: Richard Neile, Bishop of Coventry and Lichfield; writ under James I
victims.allegation: Burned for anti-Trinitarian and other heresies; the last person burned for heresy in England.

victims.name: William Laud
victims.executed: Beheaded on Tower Hill, London, 10 January 1645
victims.condemned_by: The Long Parliament, by ordinance of attainder
victims.allegation: Accused of trying to subvert the laws and the Protestant religion.

victims.name: Charles I
victims.condemned_by: High Court of Justice set up by the Rump Parliament
victims.allegation: Convicted of treason against the people; the conflict was partly religious, and the Church of England later honored him as a martyr.
victims.verification_note: The execution is certain; how far it was a religious rather than a political act is debated.

victims.name: John Southworth
victims.executed: Hanged, drawn, and quartered at Tyburn, London, 28 June 1654
victims.allegation: Executed for being a Catholic priest in England, after admitting his priesthood.

victims.name: Edward Coleman
victims.executed: Hanged, drawn, and quartered at Tyburn, London, 3 December 1678
victims.condemned_by: Court of King's Bench under Chief Justice Scroggs
victims.allegation: First victim of the Popish Plot; his letters seeking French help for Catholicism were used as proof of the invented plot.

victims.name: William Howard, Viscount Stafford
victims.executed: Beheaded on Tower Hill, London, 29 December 1680
victims.allegation: Convicted on informers' evidence of plotting to kill the king in the Popish Plot.

victims.name: Oliver Plunkett
victims.executed: Hanged, drawn, and quartered at Tyburn, London, 1 July 1681
victims.condemned_by: Court of King's Bench in London on informers' evidence
victims.allegation: Catholic archbishop of Armagh convicted of plotting a French invasion of Ireland; the last Catholic executed for the faith at Tyburn, canonized in 1975.

victims.name: James Renwick
victims.executed: Hanged in the Grassmarket, Edinburgh, 17 February 1688
victims.condemned_by: Scottish High Court of Justiciary under James VII
victims.allegation: Covenanter field preacher who denied the king's authority; usually called the last Covenanter martyr.
